node.label: Steven Shapin
node.date_label: Leviathan and the Air-Pump (with Simon Schaffer) (1985) · A Social History of Truth (1994) · The Scientific Revolution (1996)
node.description: A historian of science who studies how trust, personal character and institutions sustain knowledge. His Scientific Life interview questions sharp distinctions between academic virtue and industrial self-interest, and argues that scientific uncertainty can make personal credibility more important.

named_group_routes.relationship: Sociologists of scientific knowledge answer that their methodological relativism was misread as hostility to science (1996–97)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period replies in the sociologists' own words. Collins and Pinch, letter in Physics Today 49:7 (1996), p. 11, answering Mermin: "Many scientists, especially those who have become spokespersons, are evidently scientific fundamentalists. ... Where we sociologists think of ourselves as trying to gain social and historical insight into science, the fundamentalists see heresy"; The Golem is "about as inoffensive a social analysis of science as one could wish for"; they cite historical work on the slow reception of relativity. Mermin replied on the same page that "the rightness/wrongness axis is not a relevant dimension in their kind of sociological analysis of science". David Edge, "The Umpire Strikes Back" (EASST web text, February 1997; read in a web reproduction): "A powerful group of American scientists, apparently for political reasons, have chosen to mount a vicious attack on those scholars whom they take to be 'flying from science and reason'. One of their prime targets is 'social constructivism'"; the Edinburgh group "has always maintained that reality plays a central role in what comes to be believed about it". Edge is not on the ssk roster; he is on this debate's roster. Shapin's 1999 defence of methodological relativism is carried by the science → sciencewars edge. Bloor's own reply to the warriors was not found; his 1999 complaint that Latour joined "the recent contributors to The Flight from Science and Reason" is on the ssk → latour edge.

named_group_routes.relationship: Historians of science answer the charge that their field is hostile to or ignorant of science (1996–99)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period replies by historians of science, read. Steven Shapin, "Rarely Pure and Never Simple" (Configurations 7, 1999), writing as "a historian and a sociologist of science": methodological relativism "implies nothing at all about epistemological evaluations or ontological judgments" (pp. 3–4); the charge of hostility to science or ignorance of it, "—when directed to the work of many distinguished historians and sociologists of science—now deserves to be called by its proper name: it is malevolently misinformed" (p. 11). He names no protagonist; his target is identified by its arguments, such as Sokal's challenge to jump from a window. John Krige (Physics World, December 1998): Intellectual Impostures "is essentially a political tract" and "lamentably indifferent to the history and philosophy of science". Mara Beller (Physics Today 51:9, 1998): "The philosophical pronouncements of Bohr, Born, Heisenberg and Pauli deserve some of the blame for the excesses of the postmodernist critique of science." M. Norton Wise reviewed Higher Superstition in Isis (1996; unread); Edge reports his charge of "a willful strategy of distortion and demonization" (p. 323). Jardine and Frasca-Spada (SHPS 1997) criticised both sides and are not counted as one-way critics. Not every historian of science sided against the warriors: Margaret Jacob wrote against Latour in A House Built on Sand (1998; see the truthdebate → latour edge). Physicists also criticised historians' method (Weinberg 1996 on Whig history; Sokal and Bricmont 1998, p. 69 n. 88); that thinner charge is not drawn as a sciencewars → science edge. The arrow targets the debate as a whole: these historians answered the attackers' arguments (Gross and Levitt, Sokal, Sokal and Bricmont, Weinberg), not the respondents' strand in which they sit.

named_group_routes.relationship: Appleby, Hunt and Jacob judge the strong programme's relativism inadequate to historical and scientific truth (1994)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The historians' own words: Telling the Truth about History (1994), read in the Norton 2011 e-book, which has no print page numbers; cited by chapter. Ch. 5 ("Discovering the Clay Feet of Science"): the social constructionists "could not explain the way in which technical problems, or new natural phenomena like viruses, set whole research agendas"; the social insight "does not, however, underwrite the more extreme claims of strong programmers who have never offered an adequate theory to address the complexity of circumstances and situations that produce reasonably true human knowledge"; "relativism fails the needs of historians just as it skirts the possible existence of truths in science" (n. 24 cites Barnes and Bloor, "Relativism, Rationalism and the Sociology of Knowledge"). Ch. 7 calls social constructionists "once called strong programmers". The book was published in 1994, before the 1996 hoax. No SSK reply to it was found; Shapin's 1999 complaint that methodological relativism is "routinely misrepresented" (n. 6) is a general answer, not a reply to this book. Print pages remain to be checked.

named_group_routes.relationship: Bloor answers that Latour misrepresents the Strong Program and that his own alternative is "obscurantism" (1999); Collins and Yearley had called the actor-network approach a "backward step" (1992)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Bloor's own words, read in "Anti-Latour" (SHPS 30, 1999): "Bruno Latour is a vehement critic of the sociology of knowledge in general, and the Strong Program in particular" (p. 81); "I think Latour is wrong ... If anything they are a step backwards" (p. 82); "his criticisms are based on a systematic misrepresentation of the position he rejects, and ... his own approach, in so far as it is different, is unworkable" (p. 82); the charge that SSK explains nature by society "is a profound misrepresentation. The aim isn't to explain nature, but to explain shared beliefs about nature" (p. 87); Latour's vocabulary of actants "looks like a formula for imposing confusion on ourselves: it is obscurantism raised to the level of a general methodological principle" (p. 97); "Latour has endorsed, and encouraged, a wholly false stereotype of the Strong Program", joining "the recent contributors to The Flight from Science and Reason" (pp. 110–111). He partly concedes: "Latour, rightly, rejects the symmetry principle understood in this way" (p. 84). He cites other critiques he finds "devastating" (p. 95), including Collins and Yearley (1992), Schaffer (1991) and Shapin (1988), none read here. Collins and Yearley's chapter is known only through Callon and Latour's quotations (1992, p. 347): "The consequences of the semiotic method [of Latour] amount to a backward step". Latour's reply acknowledges the charge: "The result is a devastating critique" (1999, p. 113) and calls Schaffer's similar critique "exactly as ill-conceived" (n. 6). Bloor's rejoinder (SHPS 30, pp. 131–136) was not located.

named_group_routes.relationship: Kuhn calls the strong programme's claims "absurd: an example of deconstruction gone mad" (1991)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Kuhn's own words, read: "The Trouble with the Historical Philosophy of Science" (Rothschild Lecture, Harvard, 19 November 1991; published 1992; in The Road Since Structure, 2000): "I am among those who have found the claims of the strong program absurd: an example of deconstruction gone mad. And the more qualified sociological and historical formulations that currently strive to replace it are, in my view, scarcely more satisfactory" (p. 110); the strong program "has been widely understood as claiming that power and interest are all there are" (p. 110). In the 1995 Athens interview (same volume) he says of Shapin and Schaffer's Leviathan and the Air-Pump, "The scholarship is often damn good!", while objecting that they "totally miss" the barometer's "vastly greater explanatory power" (pp. 316–317); that remark concerns the science roster's practice strand and is context only. No SSK reply to the lecture was read. The SSK reading of Kuhn ran the other way, as appropriation (Barnes, T. S. Kuhn and Social Science, 1982, unread); edge_132 (kuhn → ssk, influence) stays.

named_group_routes.relationship: Moral economies of science: certain forms of empiricism, quantification and objectivity “require” a web of affect-saturated values (1995)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, read (Osiris 10, 1995, pp. 3–4). "certain forms of empiricism, quantification, and objectivity itself are not simply compatible with moral economies; they require moral economies" (p. 3); a moral economy is "a web of affect-saturated values that stand and function in well-defined relationship to one another" (p. 4). n. 2 gathers studies by Hannaway, Porter, Schaffer and Shapin under the rubric. A distinct contribution from the 1992 image article (edge_761); the later book Objectivity (2007, with Galison) is dated in the chronology and read only through a reviewer.
